item.title: The memory crunch sinks phone shipments, Taiwan moves to criminalize AI chip smuggling, and Amazon keeps shutting out shopping agents
item.description:
Six stories from the past week across planning, trade, manufacturing, freight, warehousing and sourcing. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
PlanningSupply chain for AI

1. AI's appetite for memory just caused the worst quarter on record for smartphones

IDC's preliminary numbers show global smartphone shipments fell 22% year over year in the third quarter to about 255 million units, the steepest quarterly drop it has ever recorded. IDC blames the AI-driven memory shortage: memory costs are up roughly 350% from a year ago, and vendors have cut low-end models and raised prices. IDC expects pressure to last through 2027 and warns that some makers built ahead of next year's expected component squeeze, which could leave excess inventory if demand stays soft.

So what for plannersIf any of your products use DRAM or flash, treat memory as a constrained, fast-moving cost input in your plan. Re-run 2027 demand and cost scenarios with current memory pricing, watch for customers pulling back on budget models, and be careful not to build inventory ahead of a squeeze that weak demand may never absorb.

#memory#chips#data centers#forecasting

Sources: 9to5Mac Independent reporting · Mobile World Live Independent reporting · FoneArena Independent reporting

TradeSupply chain for AI

2. Taiwan plans to make unauthorized AI chip shipments to China a crime

Taiwan's economics minister, Kung Ming-hsin, told Bloomberg that Taipei will add AI servers and leading-edge semiconductors to its list of controlled goods, in line with commitments under its trade agreement with the US. Once the change takes effect, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization would become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act. Today, Taiwan can only pursue suspected smugglers under other laws. No start date has been given.

So what for trade compliance teamsExpect tighter screening on AI servers and accelerators that ship from or through Taiwan. Check that your end-use and end-user documentation for this hardware is complete, ask your distributors how they plan to comply, and build some extra lead time into orders while the new rules are being set up.

#export controls#chips

Sources: Bloomberg Independent reporting · The Straits Times Independent reporting

ManufacturingSupply chain for AI

3. Adani and Jabil sign up to build AI racks and servers in India

Adani Enterprises and contract manufacturer Jabil signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding on October 13 for a 50:50 joint venture to make and assemble AI racks, servers, storage, networking gear, power distribution, liquid cooling and transformers in India, plus installation and commissioning. The companies are aiming for multi-gigawatt rack capacity for Indian and export customers. No investment figure or production date was given, and the deal still needs definitive agreements and approvals.

So what for supply chain managersAnother region is lining up to build AI data-center hardware, which could widen your options for racks, power and cooling over time. Note it on your supplier map, but don't count on it as capacity until there's a signed JV, a plant and a qualified product.

#AI hardware#data centers#manufacturing capacity

Sources: Adani Enterprises release Company announcement · CNBC-TV18 Independent reporting · Voice&Data Independent reporting

LogisticsAI in supply chain

4. Kodiak's autonomous trucks now run reefer and dry freight to Laredo

Kodiak AI and carrier Charger Logistics are hauling refrigerated and dry-van freight for food, beverage and consumer-goods shippers on the 435-mile lane between Dallas and Laredo, the busiest US land port of entry. The first load ran September 8, and a safety driver is still on board until Kodiak finishes its safety case. Charger owns the trucks and runs Kodiak's driving system under a driver-as-a-service model, and it has a separate autonomy deal with Aurora on the same lane.

So what for logistics leadsAutonomous capacity is reaching cross-border feeder lanes, not just Dallas to Houston. If you move freight toward Laredo, ask carriers which loads might ride autonomous trucks, how handoffs to Mexican carriers work, and what changes in tracking, liability and service commitments.

#autonomous trucks#freight

Sources: Kodiak AI news release Company announcement · FreightWaves Independent reporting · CCJ Independent reporting

WarehousingAI in supply chain

5. Robots are sorting Zalando's fashion returns without item-by-item training

Sereact's two-armed robots are now sorting Zalando returns in live operations at CEVA Logistics sites in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland. Sereact says its Cortex software lets the robots pick, identify and sort crumpled items they've never seen, without per-product setup or a fixed item list. The system is sold as robotics-as-a-service, and staff move to supervising stations, handling exceptions and checking quality. The companies call it the first step toward automating returns across Europe.

So what for warehouse managersReturns are among the hardest jobs to automate, so this is a useful test case. If returns volume is a pain point, ask vendors for live rates on mixed, messy items, what share of items still fall to people, and how pricing works under a service contract.

#robotics#warehouse automation#returns

Sources: Sereact announcement Company announcement · The Next Web Independent reporting · International Transport Journal Independent reporting

ProcurementAI in supply chain

6. Amazon keeps blocking outside AI shopping agents, and now Grok Bot hits the wall

On October 15, users posted screenshots showing xAI's Grok Bot being stopped from ordering on Amazon with a notice that access by an unauthorized AI agent breaks Amazon's Conditions of Use. Elon Musk replied that users could buy elsewhere and floated starting an Amazon competitor, without giving details. Amazon hasn't publicly commented on Grok Bot, but it confirmed last month that it blocked Meta's Muse agent and is fighting Perplexity in court, arguing that agents should identify themselves and get the store's agreement.

So what for procurement leadersAgent-driven buying will depend on which sellers and marketplaces let agents in. Before you pilot AI agents for purchasing, check each supplier's terms on automated ordering, favor channels with official agent or punchout integrations, and keep a person approving orders and payment details.

#AI agents#agentic commerce

Sources: Teslarati Independent reporting · Investing.com Independent reporting · GeekWire (Muse block) Independent reporting

Tip of the DayFor Supply chain managers

Use AI to run a quick what-if on your riskiest single-source parts

Pick the ten items where one supplier or one region would hurt most if it went down. Give your approved AI assistant an anonymized table of those items and ask it to walk through a four-week outage for each: what runs out first, what it costs, and which fallback buys the most time. It won't replace a full risk model, but it turns a vague worry into a ranked list you can act on this quarter.

You are a supply chain risk analyst. Below are our 10 highest-exposure items (anonymized): item code, supplier code, supplier region, weeks of stock on hand, weekly usage, lead time in weeks, whether an alternate source is qualified (Y/N), and margin impact per week of lost output.
[PASTE TABLE]
Scenario: the supplier for each item is unable to ship for [NUMBER] weeks.
1) For each item, estimate the week we run out and the total margin at risk. Show your math.
2) Rank the items by margin at risk.
3) For the top 3, suggest two realistic mitigations (for example: buffer stock, qualify an alternate, re-sequence production) and roughly what each would cost or require.
4) List any data that's missing or looks inconsistent instead of guessing.
Use a table for steps 1 and 2. Keep the whole answer under 300 words.

item.title: TSMC says AI chip demand still outruns supply, robot trucks take on routine freight, and robot brains go on tap
item.description:
Eight stories from the past week across freight, warehousing, factories, planning, sourcing and trade. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
ManufacturingSupply chain for AI

1. TSMC: AI chip demand is still bigger than its capacity, and it's scouting Texas

TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of about $46.7B, up roughly 51% from a year ago, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $52.3B to $54.3B. Management said AI-related demand remains very strong and the gap between demand and supply is still large, with 2026 capital spending planned at $60B to $64B. The WSJ reported that TSMC has sent teams to Texas to evaluate expansion beyond Arizona.

So what for buyersDon't plan on leading-edge chip or advanced-packaging lead times easing in 2027. For anything with AI accelerators or high-end logic inside, keep forecasts current with your distributors, confirm allocation in writing, and ask which builds depend on CoWoS packaging capacity.

#chips#manufacturing capacity#data centers#lead times

Sources: TSMC press release Company announcement · Wall Street Journal Independent reporting

LogisticsAI in supply chain

2. A Texas carrier adds Waabi's autonomous trucks to haul repeat freight

Warrior Logistics, an asset-based carrier with 200+ trucks, is running recurring food, beverage and consumer-goods loads on Waabi Driver-powered trucks between Dallas and Houston. Waabi says those routes have so far delivered 100% on-time pickup and delivery with no safety incidents, though neither company shared truck or load counts. Waabi also says its load volume on the lane is up more than 80% this year.

So what for logistics leadsAutonomous capacity is showing up on steady, repeatable Texas lanes first. If you ship regular freight in that corridor, ask your carriers whether autonomous trucks are in their network, and how service levels, liability and tracking change on those loads.

#autonomous trucks#freight

Sources: FreightWaves Independent reporting · AJOT Independent reporting

WarehousingAI in supply chain

3. Ultra raises $50M to lease packing robots to warehouses by the month

Brooklyn-based Ultra closed a $50M Series A led by Framework Ventures, bringing total funding to $62M. It installs its OP1 packing robots at warehouses and third-party logistics sites for an upfront integration fee plus a monthly service fee, rather than a big capital purchase. The company says its robots have packed over 500,000 orders, and it relies on Physical Intelligence for the AI models that run them.

So what for warehouse managersRobots-as-a-service turns automation into an operating expense you can pilot. Before signing, pin down the trial terms, uptime and throughput guarantees, who handles exceptions the robot can't, and what happens to pricing at renewal.

#robotics#warehouse automation#funding

Sources: Fortune Independent reporting · SiliconANGLE Independent reporting · Post on X: x.com/fundable_ai/status/2110383841923981386 Post on X

PlanningAI in supply chain

4. Kao's AI agent drafts demand plans, and people still make the call

In an English release this week, Japanese consumer-goods maker Kao detailed Kao-MIKOMIL, an AI agent that layers planned promotions, channels and pricing on top of forecasts from its in-house AI forecasting model, then proposes a demand plan with its reasoning. Business staff review and approve the plan. It went live for the KATE cosmetics brand in July and will expand to other brands, as part of Kao's goal to cut cosmetics inventory about 25% by 2027 versus 2024.

So what for plannersThe useful pattern here is the split: a forecasting model for the baseline, and an AI agent that explains how promotions and launches change it. Ask for the rationale with every AI-suggested plan, and track whether it actually beats your current forecast before you trust it.

#AI agents#forecasting

Sources: Kao news release Company announcement · ITmedia Keyman's Net (Japanese) Independent reporting

LogisticsAI in supply chain

5. Samsara opens its no-code AI agent builder to all fleet customers

Samsara made Agent Studio generally available on October 13. Fleets can build chat and voice agents on their own operating data, for example to compile reports, flag possible hours-of-service violations, or answer driver questions from company policy. Samsara says agent use is now running at about seven times its June launch pace, but it hasn't said how many customers run agents in production.

So what for logistics leadsStart with one narrow agent that has a clear owner and a checkable answer, like a daily hours-of-service risk list. Keep a person approving anything that changes a dispatch or touches a driver's record.

#AI agents#freight

Sources: Samsara press release Company announcement · FreightWaves Independent reporting

ManufacturingAI in supply chain

6. Physical Intelligence opens its robot models to outside developers

Physical Intelligence launched a waitlisted beta of its Pi API on October 13. Teams upload their own robot data, fine-tune the company's general-purpose models on its managed infrastructure, and run them through a hosted service. Robots-as-a-service provider Formic, which says 150 factories use its robots, is an early partner. The company noted that network connectivity was a challenge in some early cloud-run deployments.

So what for operations and plant managersGeneral-purpose robot AI is becoming something you rent, not build. If you evaluate it, plan for the plant network: test what happens when connectivity drops, where your production data goes, and who owns the fine-tuned model.

#robotics#AI adoption

Sources: Physical Intelligence blog Company announcement · The Robot Daily Independent reporting

ProcurementAI in supply chain

7. Scimplify raises $25M to add US capacity for specialty and critical-materials chemistry

Scimplify, a Bengaluru-based specialty chemicals and advanced materials maker, raised $25M in a round led by Hitachi Ventures, with Henkel and Teknor Apex joining. Total funding is now about $80M. It plans US research and processing capacity for areas with thin domestic supply, such as rare-earth and critical-metal purification and high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals, and will keep building its in-house AI platform for taking chemistry from lab to production.

So what for procurement leadersNew suppliers for hard-to-source chemistries are forming, often backed by the customers who need them. Add players like this to your market scan, but qualify them like any new source: samples, quality systems, and proven capacity before you shift volume.

#funding#critical materials#manufacturing capacity

Sources: TechCrunch Independent reporting · Global Venturing Independent reporting · Mint Independent reporting · Post on X: x.com/Inc42/status/2110648247890919640 Post on X

TradeSupply chain for AI

8. Chip tariffs: the data-center exemption is still in limbo

January's Section 232 tariff put 25% on certain advanced logic chips but exempted chips headed for US data centers, pending a Commerce Department review that hasn't been published. On October 2, five tech trade groups including CCIA and TechNet asked the White House to keep any further chip, robotics and machinery tariffs targeted, and to extend any tariff offset program to downstream buyers. No second-phase decision has been announced.

So what for trade compliance teamsIf you import servers, accelerators or robotics, map which items fall under the current tariff codes and which end-use exemption you rely on. Keep the paperwork for that exemption ready, and model landed cost both with and without it.

#tariffs#chips#data centers

Sources: The White House proclamation Government document · CCIA Industry association · The Next Web Independent reporting

Tip of the DayFor Logistics and warehouse teams

Use AI to audit freight invoices against what you agreed to pay

Accessorial charges like detention, lumper and liftgate fees are where freight bills quietly drift. Each week, export invoiced charges next to the rate confirmation for the same loads, swap carrier and customer names for neutral codes, and have your approved AI assistant flag every mismatch. You still decide what to dispute, but the AI does the line-by-line comparison.

You are a freight audit assistant. Below are this week's loads (anonymized). For each load: load ID, carrier code, lane, agreed linehaul, agreed fuel surcharge %, agreed accessorials, then invoiced linehaul, invoiced fuel, and invoiced accessorials with amounts.
[PASTE TABLE]
1) Compare invoiced to agreed for every load and list each mismatch with the dollar difference.
2) Flag accessorials that weren't on the rate confirmation, and any detention billed without times shown.
3) Total the overbilled amount by carrier code.
4) Draft a short, polite dispute note for the three largest mismatches, with [PLACEHOLDERS] for names.
Use a table for step 1 and don't guess at missing values; list them separately.

item.title: AI hardware is sold out, agents are learning to shop, and the financing bill is coming due
item.description:
Seven stories from the past week that matter to buyers, sourcing leads and supply chain planners. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
ManufacturingSupply chain for AI

1. Lumentum says its AI optics are sold out until about 2029

The CEO of optical-components maker Lumentum told Bloomberg the company is fully booked into early 2029. For some product lines, it can't fill about 70% of demand through 2027, and some customers are already placing orders for 2030. Six months ago, he expected to sell out only through 2028.

So what for buyersIf you buy networking or server hardware, ask distributors now about allocation and lead times on anything with high-speed optics. Put forecasts in early, and get second-source quotes before a 52-week lead time lands on you.

#optics#data centers#lead times

Sources: Japan Times / Bloomberg Independent reporting · Business Insider Independent reporting

ManufacturingSupply chain for AI

2. Adani and Jabil plan a 50:50 AI hardware joint venture in India

Adani Enterprises and contract manufacturer Jabil signed a non-binding MoU to build and assemble AI racks, servers, storage, networking, power and liquid-cooling gear in India at multi-gigawatt scale. The deal still needs definitive agreements and approvals, and no timeline has been announced.

So what for supply chain managersTreat this as a possible new source of data-center hardware supply from 2028 onward, not today's capacity. Note it in your long-range sourcing map and check again when there's a definitive agreement.

#AI hardware#manufacturing capacity#data centers

Sources: Adani press release Company announcement · Economic Times Independent reporting

ProcurementSupply chain for AI

3. GPU rental prices keep rising even as AI token prices fall

Posts on X highlighted that rental prices for top-end Nvidia GPUs climbed after per-token AI prices peaked, a classic Jevons effect: cheaper AI drives more usage. Silicon Data's B300 rental index launched near $6.95/GPU-hour, up roughly 44% since April. A separate marketplace tracker showed another weekly gain in early October.

So what for procurement leadersCheaper per-token AI doesn't mean a smaller AI bill. Write usage caps, price-review clauses and reserved-versus-on-demand comparisons into AI and cloud contracts before renewals.

#GPU compute#pricing#data centers

Sources: Silicon Data B300 index Research/data · AIMC weekly GPU market Research/data

ProcurementSupply chain for AI

4. Broadcom is lining up $30–50B+ to finance OpenAI's custom chips

The WSJ reported that Broadcom is working to arrange more than $50B in financing for the custom AI chips it is co-developing with OpenAI, with Apollo and Blackstone in talks. Bloomberg put the figure nearer $30B and called the talks early. Either way, private credit is now funding chip supply directly.

So what for supply chain managersWhen suppliers finance their biggest customers' purchases, allocation follows the money for years. Map which of your critical inputs share constrained AI chip and server capacity, and build distributor and tier-2 relationships now.

#chips#funding#data centers

Sources: Business Times (WSJ report) Independent reporting · Bloomberg Law Independent reporting

ProcurementAI in supply chain

5. Shopify lets AI agents shop and check out, with spending limits

Shopify's Shop skill and Shop MCP let personal AI agents search a catalog of over 1 billion products, build carts and complete Shop Pay checkout. Shoppers approve purchases, or can set budgets that let the agent pay without asking. Shopify also reported its ecosystem supported 9.6M+ jobs in the year to June 2026.

So what for procurement leadersAgent buying is arriving in consumer checkout first. Start drafting policy for agent-placed purchases: approval limits, which suppliers are allowed, and audit trails. Ask key suppliers whether their catalogs and pricing are readable by machines.

#AI agents#agentic commerce

Sources: Shopify developer changelog Company announcement · Shop Help Center Company announcement

PlanningAI in supply chain

6. TikTok tests an AI shopping assistant and one-click Buy Direct

TikTok is rolling out a conversational shopping assistant and Buy Direct, an in-feed checkout, to eligible advertisers. Integrations include Salesforce, Shopify and Stripe.

So what for plannersWhen demand moves into AI chat and social feeds, promotion spikes can arrive with little warning. Add these channels as demand signals, and watch for pull-forward and the dip that follows.

#agentic commerce#AI agents

Sources: TikTok Newsroom Company announcement · TechCrunch Independent reporting · Post on X: x.com/igor_pesin/status/2107681739405447420 Post on X

ProcurementAI in supply chain

7. Practitioner tip: "boring AI" is the procurement win

A procurement practitioner described the most useful AI agent job in a single line: read supplier offers, compare them with your requirements, and flag what's missing. It's a narrow, checkable task, as opposed to an autonomous buyer.

So what for buyersStart with bid comparison and gap-finding on RFQ responses: a narrow task you can check. Keep award decisions human, and use only data your company has approved for AI tools.

#AI adoption#AI agents

Post on X: x.com/marcrojek/status/2108527900677001485 Post on X · Opinion post

Tip of the DayFor Material managers

Have AI review your stock-out exceptions, not the whole stock list

Each morning, export only the parts that are below their reorder point or have past-due receipts, with item IDs swapped for neutral codes. Paste that short list into your approved AI assistant and ask it to sort by risk and draft one follow-up question per part. Then you spend your time on the five calls that matter instead of scanning hundreds of lines.

You are a materials planning assistant. Below is today's exception list (anonymized): part code, on-hand, reorder point, average daily usage, open PO qty, PO due date, supplier lead time in days.
[PASTE TABLE]
1) Calculate days of supply for each part and flag any that will run out before the next PO arrives.
2) Rank the parts by stock-out risk (highest first) and show your math.
3) For the top 5, draft one short, specific question to ask the supplier or buyer.
4) List any rows where the data looks inconsistent.
Keep it under 250 words, and use a table for step 2.
